finale.text: Thirteen stops and the trick shows up everywhere. The Departed's police headquarters was the state employment office; its penthouse is a law library. Cheers was a door on Beacon Street and a room in Hollywood. Spotlight's newsroom was a Toronto warehouse. Glory's 1860s Boston was mostly Savannah. Thomas Crown came home to a Bulfinch house and, often, a soundstage. What Boston actually supplies is the outside: the concrete, the steps, the cobblestones, the wharf, and one bench by a lagoon that nobody ever had to label. The outside keeps going, too. A few minutes up Summer Street from South Station is the corner where the Great Fire of 1872 started, in a basement.

pitch_60: The bar from Cheers was in Hollywood. The door is on Beacon Street, and the owner, by one account, charged a dollar to use it. That's the trick Boston pulls in every movie: the outside is real, and the inside gets built somewhere else. Shot Here is a free walk past thirteen stops, twelve of them real film and TV locations. The Departed's state police headquarters, which the state built for its employment office. The crooked cop's penthouse, which is a law library. The firehouse that fire historians say a TV detective moved into. A real bank where a film crew staged a robbery in nineteen sixty-seven, and a student paper says the doors are still there. A little square that played a video-game city one summer and old New York three years later. A ship blown up in the harbor that broke windows in East Boston. Every stop is a riddle, and every answer is something you read off the street. Every fact has a source. It starts at Government Center. Bring good shoes for Beacon Hill.

seo.landing_copy:
Every Boston movie fan knows the front of the bar from Cheers. Fewer know that the room you watched for eleven years was a soundstage in Hollywood, and the real pub's basement doesn't look much like it. That's the pattern this walk is built on: Boston plays itself from the outside, and the insides get built somewhere cheaper.

Shot Here is a self-guided walking hunt through Boston's real film and TV locations. It starts at Government Center, at the concrete building The Departed turned into a police headquarters, and climbs over Beacon Hill to the house Thomas Crown came home to and the old firehouse that fire historians say a TV detective moved into. Then it drops down to Beacon Street and the Public Garden - the Cheers steps, Make Way for Ducklings in bronze, and the Good Will Hunting bench, which has no sign and doesn't need one. From the top of the Common it heads downtown, past a penthouse that's really a library and a gold door a student paper ties to Thomas Crown's bank job, to the square that played a video-game city and old New York, and out to the harbor.

Each stop is a riddle that walks you to the next location, and the answer is something you can only get by looking: a name on a building, a number over a door, a word in bronze. Then you get the story - what was filmed there, what wasn't, and where the famous version is wrong.

We stick to places you can stand on a public sidewalk at any hour, and to facts we can source: the American Film Institute's catalog, the Boston Globe, American Cinematographer, Boston.com, the Boston Fire Historical Society, Mass Humanities, the National Park Service. Every source is listed. Where sources disagree, we say so. No stills, no scripts, no spoilers beyond what the street already gives away.

Thirteen stops, about two and three-quarter hours and five and a half kilometers, with a one-hour short cut through Beacon Hill and the Public Garden. Part of Off the Bricks: Boston Hunts.

web_page.intro: Boston plays itself from the outside. The Cheers bar was a set on Paramount Stage 25 in Hollywood. The Departed's State Police headquarters was built for the state's employment office. Most of Glory's 1860s Boston was Savannah. Here are thirteen real locations you can stand in front of, from Government Center over Beacon Hill to the harbor, each with its sources. Off the Bricks turns them into a walk, with a riddle at every stop.

stops.public_fact: The Departed's State Police headquarters is the Hurley Building, which the state built for its Division of Employment Security.
Thomas Crown's Beacon Hill house was designed by Charles Bulfinch for Harrison Gray Otis, who later became Boston's third mayor.
The Boston Fire Historical Society says the old Engine 10 firehouse on Mount Vernon Street was Spenser's home on TV, and MTV's Real World used it in 1997.
Mass Moments says Cheers was shot mostly on Paramount Stage 25 in Hollywood; Beacon Street supplied the outside.
In July 1991 a copy of the Public Garden's duckling sculpture went to Moscow's Novodevichy Park as a gift to Soviet children.
Boston.com noted in 2025 that no sign tells you which bench by the Public Garden lagoon is the one from Good Will Hunting.
The American Film Institute says Savannah, Georgia, stood in for most of Glory's 1860s Boston.
Colin Sullivan's penthouse in The Departed is the top-floor library of Suffolk University Law School, facing the Common.
Director Norman Jewison said the Thomas Crown Affair's bank robbery was shot at a downtown branch of the National Shawmut Bank.
Boston.com reported Free Guy dressing Liberty Square as Free City in 2019, and Madame Web making it a retro New York Chinatown in 2022.
A Cheers bar built as a replica of the TV set poured at Faneuil Hall Marketplace from 2001 until August 30, 2020.
In September 1993 Blown Away staged a ship explosion in Boston Harbor that the Globe said shattered East Boston windows.
The Boston Redevelopment Authority bought South Station in 1965 and decided to tear it down, Amtrak's station history says.

story.card_text: The Departed's State Police headquarters was never a police building. In the 2006 film this concrete complex plays the outside of the special investigations unit, and Boston.com and Suffolk University's student paper both name the Hurley Building, the half of the block nearer Cambridge Street. The state built it for its Division of Employment Security, later used it for labor and workforce offices, and says it is now empty. The other half, the Erich Lindemann Mental Health Center, still houses the Department of Mental Health. Paul Rudolph sketched the whole Government Service Center as one plan in 1962; it was never fully built, and both buildings were finished by 1971. The most Boston movie of its decade is also a remake of a Hong Kong film, Infernal Affairs (2002), adapted by Dorchester-born William Monahan, and it won four Oscars. The live story here is real estate: the state took redevelopment offers for the block until September 18, 2026, and says they are under review. Look at the concrete stair that climbs from the Staniford Street sidewalk to the plaza.

story.card_text: Two TV shows moved into this firehouse, by the fire historians' account. The Boston Fire Historical Society says it was the home of the title character in Spenser: For Hire, the Boston detective show that ran from 1985 to 1988 with Robert Urich, and that MTV's The Real World used it for its Boston season in 1997. In the show, Spenser lived in an unused Beacon Hill firehouse for part of the run; the Somerville Times says Boston's firefighters gave it to him. The show didn't have to fake much. Firefighters had worked this corner since August 1847, when a hand engine company was organized here. The building you're looking at went up from 1946 and Engine 10 moved in in April 1949, in a building planned to fit bigger fire trucks. Engine 10 left in 1982 for 123 Oliver Street downtown, and a fire safety chief worked out of here until the department gave the building up in 1995 - so when Spenser moved in on TV, it was still a fire department building. It's been Hill House, the neighborhood's community center, since 1998.

story.card_text: Most of Glory's 1860s Boston is Savannah, Georgia. The American Film Institute's catalog says the Georgia city stood in for Boston, with some exteriors shot on Beacon Hill, and Fort Wagner was rebuilt on Jekyll Island. This bronze is the part that's real: the Beacon Hill Times noted in 2019 that it appears in the film's closing credits. The real regiment - 1,007 Black soldiers and 37 white soldiers, by the Beacon Hill Times' count - gathered on this Common on May 28, 1863, and marched down Beacon Street past William Lloyd Garrison, Wendell Phillips and Frederick Douglass. Their colonel, Robert Gould Shaw, was killed leading the assault on Fort Wagner, South Carolina, on July 18. Augustus Saint-Gaudens spent nearly fourteen years on the memorial, and it was unveiled on May 31, 1897. The film's Black soldiers are composite characters, not historical men of the 54th. It won three Oscars, including Denzel Washington's for supporting actor. In January 1990 city and state officials marked a Glory Day with a ceremony that began at this memorial.

Augustus Saint-Gaudens worked on this for nearly fourteen years, and it was unveiled in eighteen ninety-seven. story.card_text: The city bought South Station in 1965 and decided to knock it down. Amtrak's station history says the Boston Redevelopment Authority paid nearly $7 million for it, and a 1972 Boston Globe Magazine story reported the plan to tear down the rest and replace it with new development. It survived: the station went on the National Register of Historic Places in 1975 and was renovated in the 1980s. That's lucky for this walk. South Station opened on New Year's Day 1899, designed by the Boston firm Shepley, Rutan and Coolidge, and the Boston Globe's list of Boston film locations puts it in two movies you've already met: The Thomas Crown Affair glimpsed it in 1967, and The Verdict filmed at it in 1982. Now look up at the top of the curve. The clock is styled after Big Ben, with a twelve-foot face, and in 2008 the Globe called it the largest operating hand-wound clock in New England. The stone eagle on top has an eight-foot wingspan, Amtrak says, and the Globe put it at more than eight tons. Nobody had to build this one on a soundstage.

walk_from_previous.directions: Walk back off Long Wharf to Atlantic Avenue and turn left (south). Follow the Greenway along Atlantic Avenue for about fifteen minutes, past Rowes Wharf, to Dewey Square at Summer Street. Two things on the way: just before Congress Street, the tall InterContinental hotel across Atlantic was designed around the Big Dig's exhaust stacks (a stop in Under Boston), and the fire alarm box on the Congress Street corner is a stop in Alarm Club's 1852 Hunt. The curved granite station with the big clock is South Station. Look at it from the square.

subtitle: Where Boston's movies were really filmed
summary: Boston's film and TV locations, and where the famous version is wrong. The Cheers bar was a set on Paramount Stage 25 in Hollywood. The Departed's State Police headquarters was built for the state's employment office, and Colin Sullivan's penthouse is a law library. This walk goes from the West End over Beacon Hill, through the Public Garden and the Common, to the Financial District and the harbor: the real doors, the real domes, and a running list of what got built somewhere else.
